sources.title: Court rules Trump can blacklist Anthropic for refusing to enable Claude features

discussion.body: The court hands the balancing act to the president and the defense secretary rather than deciding it itself, which amounts to saying the choice between those two failure modes is a question for the executive, not the judiciary.
Even-handed in framing, maybe. But the same court had already declined to pause the blacklisting back in April, well before this panel wrote out the risks on both sides.

items.title: Judges Say the US Can Blacklist Anthropic Over Withheld AI Features
items.body: Judges decided the US had authority to blacklist Anthropic technology for the company's withholding of certain AI features, and that the authority holds even if Anthropic had no malicious intent. In other words, a vendor's judgment about which capabilities to hand over does not shelter it from being cut off from government work, provided the government's action stays inside its statutory and constitutional limits — which, in this ruling, the court found it did. That is the kind of precedent that quietly reaches every company selling models to the military: the question of who decides which features are safe enough to ship now has a partial answer, and the answer favors the buyer with the biggest budget. Any vendor weighing whether to withhold a capability now has to price in the possibility of losing the whole relationship rather than just that one deal, which pushes the argument over model behavior out of procurement meetings and into the courts and the Pentagon. What makes the ruling worth reading is how it sets out the dilemma underneath the dispute. The government's concern, as the court put it, is the prospect of overly constrained AI models shutting down unexpectedly and causing important military operations to fail; Anthropic's is the prospect of unconstrained models hallucinating inappropriate targets for lethal military force. Framed that way, the case is less about one company's feature set than about which failure mode is tolerable, and who gets to choose.

sources.title: Can Trump ever be wrong? His pick to lead FDA refused to say.

items.title: Two Hours of Not Answering at the FDA Confirmation Hearing
items.body: Heidi Overton, President Trump's nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, went before the Senate health committee on Thursday to face questions about her stances on vaccines, flavored vapes, birth control and abortion, among other issues. According to Ars Technica, she spent nearly two hours stonewalling senators, even on softball questions. A nominee can reasonably decline to prejudge specific product decisions before confirmation; nobody expects an FDA hopeful to promise approvals in advance. Two hours of refusing even the easy questions is a different posture. It tells the committee that the most useful thing it will learn about how she would run the agency is whatever is already on the public record.

sources.title: Multi-Region training with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod and Qumulo

discussion.body: Cross-region reads aren't free even when throughput holds. Accessing data across regions adds transfer costs on top of latency, which is part of what pushes teams toward replicating data in the first place.

Which makes the parity result the one worth testing harder. If the latency penalty can really be absorbed, replication becomes optional rather than mandatory, and that is a much bigger change than one cluster's benchmark.

items.title: The Cross-Region Training Run That Kept Pace
items.body: Training compute and training data don't always sit in the same place. Teams have faced an awkward choice when the GPU capacity they can get and the dataset they need are in different AWS Regions: replicate petabytes of data across regions, or absorb cross-region latency on every read and accept slower training. In an AWS write-up, the company describes a validation run of the second option done properly. The same training job ran on two clusters: a hub in US East (Ohio) co-located with the data, and a spoke in US West (Oregon) reading that data remotely through Qumulo's Cloud Data Fabric, with 60 milliseconds of network latency between them. After a short warmup, the spoke matched the hub's throughput. The claim is the vendor's own, from a single validation run, so it is a promising internal result rather than independent evidence. But the shape of it is what matters: if a remote read can be made to behave like a local one, the decision to copy a dataset stops being forced and starts being a choice.

sources.title: Wrongfully detained Iranian American journalist remains jailed in Iran after 2 years

items.title: A Ten-Year Sentence After a Family Visit to Iran
items.body: This week marks two years since Iranian American journalist Reza Valizadeh was detained in Iran. For a decade he worked for Radio Farda, an independent but U.S.-funded Farsi-language news service. During a trip to Iran to visit family, he was arrested and sentenced to ten years in prison for “collaborating with a hostile government.”

sources.title: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?

discussion.body: The venue is doing work here. Framing agent security as a shared problem at the UN is more useful to a government that wants international rules than a domestic press conference would be.

Or it's just the biggest stage available. The measures Australia has proposed — algorithm controls, smart-glasses rules — are national policy, not a treaty, so the setting may be louder than the substance.

items.title: An AI Agent Hacked a Government System. Australia Made the Announcement at the UN.
items.body: An automated AI agent hacked a government IT system, BBC Technology reports — an episode that raises big questions about how the technology gets regulated. Australia announced the breach at the United Nations rather than through a domestic channel, and the venue is the interesting part of the choice. Australia already has strict social media restrictions and has proposed controls on algorithms and smart glasses; this is a government that regulates tech, not one that merely complains about it. Taking a breach to the UN casts agent security as a shared international problem rather than a single country's incident, even though the controls Australia has floated are national measures. What a useful rule would actually target is a harder question. An agent that gets into a system is a different kind of problem from the algorithm and device questions already on the table.

sources.title: Health care costs a major concern for voters ahead of midterms

discussion.body: Two separate mechanisms are in play: marketplace enrollment fell mainly because federal credits expired, while the plan to cancel coverage for nearly 760,000 people is an administration action with its own rationale.

The fraud rationale and the coverage figure should be kept apart. Claims of widespread fraud are the stated justification; the 760,000 is the number of people who would lose coverage if the plan proceeds.

items.title: Falling ACA Enrollment, and a Plan to Cancel Coverage for Nearly 760,000
items.body: Health care sits at the center of a political debate as millions of Americans struggle with rising costs, PBS NewsHour reports, and two developments show up in the same frame. Enrollment in the marketplaces created by the ACA dropped this year, mainly because federal credits expired. Separately, Vice President Vance announced plans to cancel coverage for nearly 760,000 people, citing claims of widespread fraud. Those are different kinds of fact, and the distinction matters. The enrollment decline is a reported change with a stated cause; the cancellations are a planned action resting on the administration's fraud claims. Keeping the justification and the headcount apart is the honest way to read both.

items.title: A Stanford Biology Lab, Filed Under Star Wars Locations
items.body: Star Wars has taken audiences to Tatooine, Naboo and, in Variety's framing, now to a campus biology lab at Stanford University. The film making that claim is The Love Hypothesis, which premiered on Amazon Prime on Sept 23, with Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman as romantic interests caught in a fake-dating-turned-real-love plot. The location comparison is the amusing part: a rom-com's lab bench is not a desert planet, and the franchise's list of iconic places apparently keeps room for it anyway. Whether a biology lab deserves the same billing as Tatooine is a matter of taste.

sources.title: How Datacor built self-service rental analytics with Amazon Quick Sight

discussion.body: The interesting part is where the fix landed. Nobody needed a cleverer model; the numbers just needed to stop sitting behind an IT queue.
Which is also a reason to read the case study as marketing. It's published by the vendor whose analytics tool was adopted, with contributions from the customer's own engineering and product teams.

items.title: The Data Was Behind an IT Ticket. The Fix Was a Search Bar.
items.body: For gas and welding distributors, rental billing on assets such as cylinders and bulk tanks is a significant share of revenue. The data needed to manage those assets was often locked in disconnected systems, accessible only through IT. Datacor's answer, described on Amazon's machine-learning blog, was to integrate Amazon Quick Sight into the TrackAbout solution, equipping it with interactive dashboards and a natural language search bar. The transferable lesson is about where the bottleneck sat. The constraint was who could reach the numbers, not whether the numbers existed — and a question box attached to a dashboard shortens the distance between a question and the data.

sources.title: CNN left off Air Force One for Trump's upcoming trip, White House signals in new media restriction

items.title: CNN Is Left Off Air Force One for a Presidential Trip
items.body: The White House has signaled that CNN will be left off Air Force One for President Donald Trump's Saturday trip, NPR reports, describing it as the latest media restriction in an ongoing dispute with First Amendment implications. The network is still free to cover the visit from the ground; what is withheld is a seat on the manifest. Pool travel on the president's aircraft is a finite slot that the White House decides how to allocate, which is why a single exclusion reads as a decision about access rather than about coverage.

sources.title: Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic

items.title: Tom Holland's Fred Astaire Biopic Adds Margaret Qualley and Sabrina Carpenter
items.body: Margaret Qualley and Sabrina Carpenter have joined Tom Holland in his untitled Fred Astaire biopic, Deadline reports. Holland will portray the actor and dancer, and Qualley will star as Adele Astaire. The project has had a long runway: Deadline notes it comes nearly five years after Holland first revealed he would be leading it. Cast and title are still moving in different directions, with the cast filling in while the film goes without a name.

One film is one film. Hombale's distribution machinery may account for more of that $3.5 million than the subject matter does.

items.title: Hombale Films Took a Devotional Film Abroad. It Grossed More Than $3.5 Million.
items.body: The Indian devotional film “Hanuman Ansh” has grossed more than $3.5 million outside its home territory since Hombale Films took it to international audiences, Variety reports. Hombale is the company behind the K.G.F and Kantara franchises, and Variety says it has now detailed how it engineered the run. The film was written and directed by Vishal Chaturvedi and adapted from his book. The number worth holding onto is the geography of it: more than $3.5 million earned outside the film's home market, by a distributor whose track record rests on franchise blockbusters.

items.title: An Edmonton Arrest Turns on How a Man Used Snapchat to Track Two Youths
items.body: An Edmonton man was arrested earlier this month for online child sexual exploitation, according to the Alberta Law Enforcement Response Teams. ALERT says he used Snapchat to track two related youths and threatened them into sharing sexually explicit videos of themselves. The account describes coercion built on reaching people who were already connected to each other, with the threats doing the work.

discussion.body: Two claims are getting blurred here: a ruling that costs one party an advantage it sought, and any suggestion that the replacement map is drawn more fairly. Only the first is what the report says.
Fair — but the timing is the part voters feel. The map used in the general election is not the map the primaries were run on.

items.title: Missouri Voters Will Use a Different Congressional Map Than the Primaries Did
items.body: NPR reports that the Supreme Court has blocked the Trump-backed Missouri congressional map. The outlet describes the ruling as a defeat for Republicans seeking to give their party an edge in the midterms for control of the House, and notes the practical consequence: voters will face a different map than the one used in the primaries, meaning the lines that decided the nominations are not the lines the general election will be run on.

sources.title: Melissa Barrera Would Reprise ‘Scream’ Role If Rights “Leave” Spyglass: “I Love The Franchise”

items.title: Barrera's Grievance Is With Spyglass, Not Scream
items.body: Three years after being fired from the Scream franchise, Melissa Barrera remains a fan of it, Deadline reports. Her objection is to the company that holds it: she says her issue is with Spyglass Media Group, whose leadership she says never apologized for accusing her of antisemitism. Deadline reports she was fired in 2023 for supporting “Free Palestine.” Keeping the films and the studio in separate columns is a neat distinction, and an unusual one for an actor who was pushed out to bother making.

sources.title: NASA Welcomes San Marino Signing the Artemis Accords

discussion.body: The detail worth noticing is what comes attached to the signature: signatories are offered slots for payloads, technology demonstrations and CubeSats on the way back to the Moon. That reads as participation, not just a pledge.
Or as recruitment — a principles document that also assembles a partner roster for one country's lunar program.

items.title: San Marino Becomes the 76th Artemis Accords Signatory, and NASA Ties the Accords to Moon Base Plans
items.body: San Marino became the 76th signatory to the Artemis Accords, NASA says, signing during a ceremony in the city of Rimini. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson used the announcement to connect the accords to the agency's lunar ambitions, saying President Trump has directed NASA to build a Moon Base and establish an enduring presence on the lunar surface, and that NASA is putting the accords' principles into practice as it works toward that. NASA says it has invited every signatory to participate in its return to the Moon through scientific payloads, technology demonstrations, CubeSats and other capabilities.

sources.title: APOD: 2026 September 26 – Mirrored Meteor and Milky Way

discussion.body: The counterintuitive part is that the telescope is after gamma rays while seeing only visible light — the atmosphere does the conversion.
Then the camera is doing as much work as the 23-metre mirror. A billionth-of-a-second flash is a timing problem before it is a collecting-area problem.

items.title: A 23-Metre Mirror Built to Catch a Billionth-of-a-Second Flash
items.body: The prototype Large-Sized Telescope LST-1 has a 23-metre mirror assembled from 198 hexagonal segments, with a large, high-efficiency, pixelized camera behind it. Its job is stranger than it sounds: it is designed to detect extremely brief flashes of visible light in the atmosphere — events lasting about a billionth of a second, triggered by energetic gamma rays arriving from cosmic sources such as distant active galaxies. For a telescope, that is an unusual kind of watching. The thing being studied never reaches the mirror; only its after-effect in the air does. Instead of gathering light from a faint object and letting it pile up over minutes, the instrument is built around a signal that is essentially over the moment it begins. Which is why the camera's speed matters alongside the mirror's size: an event that brief rewards timing and efficiency, not just collecting area.

sources.title: How Bulgaria become a global leader in battery storage and what this means for the country's grid and energy market?

items.title: Bulgaria Became One of the World's Most Battery-Intensive Markets in Under Two Years
items.body: Deutsche Welle reports that in under two years, Bulgaria has become one of the world's most battery-intensive energy markets. The report frames the open questions plainly: whether the surge can last, and what it will mean for conventional power generators. Two years is a short span for a grid to change character, which is what makes the second question the more interesting one. Storage arriving that fast does not arrive into an empty market — it arrives alongside the generators already there.

sources.title: Brad Pitt and David Ayer Had None of Your Typical Film Set Comforts on the Survival Thriller ‘Heart of the Beast’

discussion.body: The useful way to hear this is as a claim about attention: with fewer moving parts, each one gets more of it.
Or it is a claim about pressure. A stripped-down shoot can force decisions before there is time to be sure, which is not the same thing as making them better.

items.title: David Ayer on Why a Stripped-Down Production Makes Every Decision Bigger
items.body: On IndieWire's Filmmaker Toolkit podcast, David Ayer described the challenge of telling an adventure story about a man and his dog, and made a broader point about scale: with a production this stripped down, every decision becomes exponentially more important. That inverts the intuition that smaller means more forgiving. A project without the usual comforts does not make each choice matter less — it removes the buffer that would have absorbed a bad one. An adventure story resting on a single relationship has fewer places to hide a misstep. Whether that pressure produces sharper work or merely faster decisions is the part an audience never gets to see.

sources.title: Three Decades Ago, He Made a Documentary About Then-Boyfriend Isaac Mizrahi — Now, Douglas Keeve Is Looking Back at ‘Unzipped’

discussion.body: Making a film about your partner is an unusual kind of collaboration: the movie preserves a version of the person at a particular moment, which is not the same as preserving the relationship.
Keeve's point is more precise than that. Something ending after an event is not the same as the event causing it — he can date the breakup to the film without blaming the film for it.

items.title: He Filmed His Boyfriend's Fashion World. Then the Relationship Ended.
items.body: Douglas Keeve's 1995 documentary Unzipped followed Isaac Mizrahi, then a rising fashion figure — and Mizrahi was also Keeve's boyfriend at the time. Keeve tells IndieWire that the relationship fell apart after he made the film. His insistence that follows is the interesting part: the film, he says, is not what split them. Three decades on, he is revisiting the movie and that period of his life, a reminder that the documentary a person makes about someone close to them can outlast the relationship without having caused its end.

sources.title: Ontario students improving in math, but scores still low: EQAO data

discussion.body: The two numbers do different jobs. One tracks direction of travel, the other tracks whether students are actually where the curriculum wants them. Both can be true in the same report.
True, but a year of gains from a low base is the kind of result that gets read as a turnaround. The standards figure is what keeps that reading honest.

items.title: Ontario Math Scores Improved, and Still Trail the Provincial Standard
items.body: Ontario students are showing progress in math compared with last year, CBC reports, citing new data from the province's standardized tests. The same data puts the percentage of students meeting provincial standards at a low level. Improvement and proficiency are separate measures: a rising score can sit well below the threshold the province treats as adequate, which is the gap the new numbers describe.
